newsitem.title: UK: Albright looks back to war years on London visit.
newsitem.headline: Albright looks back to war years on London visit.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright began a visit to Britain on Wednesday in which she plans to honour the past , visiting the place where Winston Churchill led the war effort while she was a Czech refugee living in air raid shelters in London.
The main purpose of her visit was talks with British leaders on such modern-day pursuits as NATO expansion plans, Bosnia peace efforts and the future of Hong Kong.

But Albright, who visited NATO headquarters on Tuesday and travels to Russia on Thursday, also planned to use her maiden visit to London as America's first female foreign minister to tour the fortified basement in Whitehall known as the cabinet war rooms.

It was there -- in a warren 10 feet (three metres) below ground -- that Churchill, then British prime minister, his cabinet, his chiefs of staff and his intelligence chiefs worked and slept from 1940 to 1945 as they plotted their responses to World War Two.

Albright, born 59 years ago in Prague to a Czech diplomat and academic, fled Czechoslovakia with her family in 1939 and stayed in Britain through the war. They later returned to their home country but after the communist takeover in 1948, fled to the United States.
"I remember spending huge portions of my life in air raid shelters singing A Hundred Green Bottles Hanging on the Wall," she told Time Magazine recently.

"I remember when we moved to Walton-on-Thames, where they had just invented some kind of a steel table. They said if your house was bombed and you were under the table, you would survive. We have this table and we ate on the table and we slept under the table and we played around the table," she said.
To another interviewer she said: "I remember the war distinctly. We were in London during the blitz. I remember what it was like to come out of the air raid shelter and see London bombed."

She could have never known then that this child of war would someday become the top diplomat for what she calls the world's "indispensable nation" with the opportunity to play a major role in shaping the post-Cold War peace.
An exponent of U.S. leadership and the use of force when necessary, Albright's views were shaped by her wartime experiences and the appeasement of Adolf Hitler at Munich.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright had no plans to visit venues in London where she formerly lived and frequented as a child. She spent Wednesday morning meeting the U.S. commander of the NATO-led forces in Bosnia and doing several media interviews, including one with British journalist David Frost, he said.
Albright later meets British Prime Minister John Major, Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind and Defence Minister Michael Portillo.
This is the fifth stop on an 11-day, nine-country tour of Europe and Asia, Albright's first overseas trip since becoming secretary of state.
The United States and Britain have the most harmonious views among the allies on security issues, including NATO expansion, U.S. officials said.

While there are disagreements on the controversial U.S. anti- Cuba law known as Helms-Burton because of its impact on European companies, officials said both sides know each other's position well and negotiations are taking place in other venues.

During her stay in Moscow, Albright is to make the latest push for Russia to conclude a charter spelling out a new relationship with NATO by the time the alliance holds a July summit in Madrid, when ex-Warsaw Pact countries will be formally invited to join NATO.
